clinicalPearls: A common flexible positional deformity of the newborn foot, usually attributed to intrauterine packaging, in which the foot is dorsiflexed and everted so that the dorsum lies against the front of the shin
The hallmark is flexibility: the foot can be passively brought down into plantarflexion and inversion, which distinguishes it from the rigid congenital vertical talus
There is no fixed bony malalignment, and radiographs, if taken, show a normally aligned talus unlike the vertical talus
Because it shares an association with in-utero moulding, the hips must be examined for developmental dysplasia, which coexists more often than by chance
Posteromedial bowing of the tibia can produce a similar calcaneovalgus posture but is accompanied by tibial angulation and a predictable leg-length discrepancy that needs monitoring
Most feet correct spontaneously within the first months of life, helped where needed by simple passive stretching taught to the parents
Persistent or more rigid deformity is uncommon and only occasionally requires serial casting
reference.pathophysiology: Calcaneovalgus foot is a soft-tissue positional deformity rather than a structural malformation, resulting from the foot being held dorsiflexed and everted in a confined intrauterine space, particularly in first pregnancies and oligohydramnios. The dorsal and lateral soft tissues are relatively contracted and the plantarflexors stretched, but the tarsal bones are normally aligned and the talonavicular joint is reduced, which is why the foot is supple and correctable. This benign packaging deformity must be separated from congenital vertical talus, in which fixed talonavicular dislocation produces a rigid rocker-bottom foot, and from posteromedial tibial bowing, where the calcaneovalgus posture accompanies a genuine tibial deformity.
additionalDifferentials: Oblique talus, an intermediate reducible deformity
Paralytic calcaneus deformity from a neuromuscular disorder
Congenital absence or deficiency of the fibula with foot valgus
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of foot flexibility and passive plantarflexion
Examination of the hips, with ultrasound for developmental dysplasia where indicated
Palpation and, if needed, radiographs of the tibia to exclude posteromedial bowing
Lateral foot radiographs only when a rigid deformity or vertical talus is suspected
Measurement and monitoring of limb length when tibial bowing is present
Neurological examination if a paralytic cause is considered
redFlags: A rigid, non-correctable foot suggesting congenital vertical talus rather than a positional deformity
Associated tibial angulation indicating posteromedial bowing with potential leg-length discrepancy
Coexisting signs of developmental dysplasia of the hip
Asymmetry or neurological signs suggesting an underlying disorder
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, as the great majority of positional calcaneovalgus feet correct spontaneously within the first few months of life, leaving a normal foot; posteromedial tibial bowing, when present, resolves its angulation but may leave a residual leg-length discrepancy requiring follow-up.
pitfalls: Confusing the supple calcaneovalgus foot with the rigid congenital vertical talus
Failing to examine the hips and missing developmental dysplasia
Overlooking posteromedial tibial bowing and its associated leg-length discrepancy
Overtreating a benign positional deformity that would resolve on its own
Alarming parents unnecessarily when simple stretching and reassurance suffice
